blocks.text: Thermohaline circulation, often called the global conveyor belt, is a crucial process in the Earth's oceans that transports heat from the tropical regions to the poles. It is driven by differences in water temperature and salinity ('thermo' for heat, 'haline' for salt), which together set the density of seawater. Warm, less dense water near the equator moves along the surface towards the polar regions, carrying heat. In polar areas the water cools and becomes denser, because of its lower temperature and the increased salinity from sea-ice formation, so it sinks and flows back towards the equator at deep ocean levels. This continuous movement helps regulate the Earth's climate, influences atmospheric patterns, and supports marine ecosystems by redistributing heat and nutrients globally.

In Fig 21.15, warm surface currents (red) flow poleward, where cooling and ice formation increase their density so that they sink (blue). This cold, dense water spreads along the ocean floor before eventually rising again in other regions. The complete three-dimensional circulation of this global conveyor belt takes approximately 1000 years to cycle water through all the world's ocean basins, and plays a crucial role in regulating the Earth's climate by redistributing heat and nutrients.

blocks.alt: A simplified loop inside a box representing the ocean. At the top a red arrow carries warm, less dense surface water from the tropics (right) towards the polar region (left). At the left, a blue arrow turns downward where water cools, sea ice forms, salinity rises and dense water sinks. Along the bottom a blue arrow carries cold deep water back towards the equator, and at the right a dashed red arrow shows it rising again (upwelling).
blocks.caption: Thermohaline circulation (original simplified diagram after Fig 21.15).
blocks.long_description: Surface water carries heat towards the poles; when it becomes cold and salty enough it sinks and returns at depth. The loop is very slow but moves an enormous amount of heat.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Thermohaline circulation, the 'global conveyor belt', takes about 1000 years to make one full cycle around the globe. If global warming slows it down, Europe could face a mini ice age, even while the rest of the world heats up.
Why does cold, salty water sink and create a deep current, and how does this relate to thermohaline circulation?
